scenario.name: incident_134_v5
scenario.title: Device Code Phishing → ARM Discovery → Exchange BEC Fraud
scenario.description:
Multi-stage Business Email Compromise (BEC) attack leveraging Azure AD device code
phishing as the initial access vector. The attacker harvests a victim executive's
OAuth token via the device code flow, performs ARM-based organizational discovery
to identify high-value wire transfer approvers, accesses the victim's Exchange Online
mailbox to gather financial context (recent invoices, payment schedules), creates
inbox rules to hide reply evidence of the compromise, and sends fraudulent wire
transfer requests impersonating the compromised executive to the finance department.
Variant 5 differentiates by using device code phishing (rather than OAuth redirect
or consent grant) and ARM-based organizational discovery for target selection.
scenario.entry_point: Device code phishing via Azure AD device code flow
scenario.final_objective: Send fraudulent wire transfer request impersonating compromised executive (BEC)

attack_paths.description:
A threat actor targets a victim executive (e.g., CFO or VP of Finance) with a device
code phishing attack. The attacker initiates the Azure AD device code flow using a
legitimate Microsoft application client ID, generating a user code. This code is
delivered to the victim via a social engineering pretext — such as a fake MFA prompt,
IT support request, or document access notification — enticing the victim to enter
the code at microsoft.com/devicelogin.

Once the victim authenticates and approves the device code, the attacker's polling
loop receives a valid OAuth access token and refresh token bound to the victim's
identity. This token grants the attacker delegated access to all resources the victim
can access, without triggering password-based alerts. The sign-in appears in
AADSignInLogs with AuthenticationProtocol=deviceCode from the attacker's IP address.

With the victim's OAuth token, the attacker queries the Azure Resource Manager (ARM)
API to perform organizational discovery. They enumerate subscriptions, resource groups,
and user directory information to identify high-value targets — specifically, employees
in the finance department who have authority to approve wire transfers. This ARM-based
discovery (rather than simple Exchange GAL enumeration) is characteristic of Variant 5
and generates AzureActivityLogs entries showing rapid GET requests across resource
providers.

Next, the attacker accesses the victim's Exchange Online mailbox via Microsoft Graph
API. They search for recent invoices, payment schedules, vendor correspondence, and
wire transfer approvals to understand the organization's financial processes, typical
transaction amounts, and communication patterns. OfficeActivity logs show bulk
MailItemsAccessed operations from the attacker's IP.

To maintain stealth, the attacker creates inbox rules on the victim's mailbox that
automatically move any replies from the identified finance targets to a hidden folder
(e.g., "RSS Subscriptions" or a custom folder). This prevents the victim from seeing
responses to the fraudulent emails, buying the attacker time. The OfficeActivity log
records a New-InboxRule operation with MoveToFolder action targeting specific senders.

mitigations.description: Train users on device-code phishing patterns and 'do not approve unsolicited prompts'.
Disable or restrict the device-code OAuth flow via Conditional Access where feasible.
Detect and block phishing links; rewrite URLs and detonate at click time.
Apply rights-management / sensitivity labels so exfiltrated mail is unreadable.
Alert on bulk user / SP enumeration via Graph.
